note.explanation: A liquid-in-glass thermometer works because its liquid expands when heated and moves up a narrow, uniform tube. The bulb transfers heat to the liquid; the tube and liquid together make the temperature readable on a scale.
examples: Mercury in a thermometer rises when its temperature increases.
A fine, uniform bore makes a small expansion easier to read on the scale.
note.checkAnswer: The narrow, uniform bore makes the liquid’s expansion correspond evenly to the scale; the thin bulb wall helps heat reach the liquid quickly.
note.simple: Heat makes the liquid in the bulb expand. It rises in the thin tube, and the scale shows the temperature.
note.checkQuestion: Why should a liquid-in-glass thermometer have a narrow, uniform tube and a thin-walled bulb?
note.title: How a Liquid-in-Glass Thermometer Works
steps: The thin wall of the glass bulb allows quick conduction through glass to the liquid from a hot object whose temperature is to be measured.
The liquid responds to the change in temperature and expands.
The uniformity of the narrow tube or bore ensures even expansion of the liquid required to make the linear measuring scale.
Read the liquid level against the scale.
note.answer: The thin bulb wall helps the liquid respond quickly to temperature changes, while the narrow, uniform bore makes its expansion readable on a linear scale.

written.finalAnswer: Sensitivity is the ability of a thermometer to respond quickly to a change in temperature.

written.text: What do you mean by the linearity of a thermometer?

written.text: Why is mercury usually preferred to alcohol as a thermometric liquid?
written.finalAnswer: Mercury is a good conductor and responds quickly to temperature changes. It also has a low freezing point and high boiling point, so it can measure over a long range. Alcohol is more expansive and can be more accurate, but its low boiling point of 78°C limits high-temperature measurements.

But alcohol has range limitation to higher temperature measurements due to its low boiling point (78°C).

written.text: What is meant by sensitive, range and linearity of thermometers? Explain with examples.
written.finalAnswer: Sensitivity describes how readily a thermometer responds to a temperature change. Range is the interval of temperatures it can measure. For example, the laboratory thermometer shown has a range from −10°C to 110°C, and its uniform bore supports a linear scale.

examTips: Board questions commonly ask you to describe the construction of a liquid-in-glass thermometer or explain why its parts are designed as they are.
For a ‘why’ question, link each feature to its function: thin bulb wall—quick conduction; fine bore—visible movement; uniform bore—even expansion and a linear scale.
When comparing mercury and alcohol, include both the advantage and limitation: mercury has a long range, while alcohol is more expansive but boils at 78°C.
In thermometer-scale numericals, first form a proportion using the fixed-point interval; show the substitution and units for method marks.

explain.title: The bulb transfers heat
explain.body: The bulb contains mercury or alcohol. Its thin glass wall allows heat to pass quickly from the object to the liquid, so the liquid can respond to the object's temperature.

explain.title: The tube makes expansion visible
explain.body: The tube is narrow and has a uniform bore. The liquid's expansion moves along this tube, and the uniform bore helps the expansion correspond evenly to the scale.

explain.title: Sensitivity and accuracy
explain.body: A small amount of liquid responds more quickly to temperature changes. The section describes mercury as sensitive for normal measurements; alcohol is more expansive and can be used for greater accuracy, but its 78°C boiling point limits higher-temperature use.

explain.title: Range of measurement
explain.body: Mercury has a low freezing point and high boiling point, so a mercury thermometer can measure over a fairly long range. The illustrated laboratory thermometer has a range from −10°C to 110°C.

mistakes: Do not say that the thermometer measures heat; it measures temperature.
Do not confuse sensitivity with range: sensitivity concerns response, while range is the interval of temperatures measurable.
Do not say that a uniform bore prevents expansion; it helps the liquid expand evenly along the scale.
Do not claim that alcohol is preferred for high temperatures; its low boiling point of 78°C is a limitation.
In scale numericals, do not use the observed length as the whole fixed-point distance; compare it with the full distance between the fixed points.
Always include the correct temperature scale unit, such as °C or °F, in the final answer.
